summary: This document extends the IMAP SEARCH and UID SEARCH commands with result options controlling what is returned, namely the minimal value, the maximal value, all matches and the count of matches. It was later updated by RFC 9394.

plainLanguage.summary: When you search your mailbox, you may want only the first match or just how many there are. This lets you ask for just that instead of the whole list.

questions: how do i get the first unseen message in imap
what does search return count do in imap
subtitle: Lets an IMAP client ask SEARCH for just the first match, last match, a count or a compact list instead of every message number.

tldr.problem: A plain IMAP SEARCH returns every matching message number, even when the client only wants the first unseen message or a count.
tldr.mechanism: The RETURN option on SEARCH and UID SEARCH selects MIN, MAX, ALL or COUNT, and the server answers with a single ESEARCH response.
tldr.outcome: Clients save bandwidth and servers can optimize MIN-only or MAX-only searches. RFC 9394 later updates it.

today: RFC 4731 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2006 and is updated by RFC 9394. It extends the IMAP protocol defined in RFC 3501.

sections.title: Why Search Results Need Options
sections.content:
An earlier document extended the IMAP SEARCH and UID SEARCH commands with result specifiers, also called result options, which control what kind of information comes back. RFC 4731 defines four of them: minimal value, maximal value, all found messages and the number of found messages.

A server that advertises the ESEARCH capability supports them. They let clients get results in more convenient forms and save bandwidth, for example by finding the first unseen message or by returning the number of unseen or deleted messages. When a single MIN or MAX is requested, the server can also optimize how it runs the search.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of reading you the whole list of matches, the helper can tell you only the first one, the last one, or how many there are.

sections.title: The Four Result Options
sections.content:
The extended commands accept these result options:

  • MIN: the lowest message number or UID that matches.
  • MAX: the highest message number or UID that matches.
  • ALL: all matching numbers or UIDs, always written in sequence-set syntax, which can be more compact and reused directly in a later command. The client MUST NOT assume any particular order.
  • COUNT: how many messages match. It MUST always be included in the ESEARCH response.

If nothing matches, the server MUST NOT include MIN, MAX or ALL, but it still MUST send the ESEARCH response. An empty option list asks for an ESEARCH response instead of SEARCH and is equivalent to (ALL).
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask for the first match, the last match, the whole list written neatly, or only how many there are.

sections.title: The ESEARCH Response
sections.content:
If one or more result options are given, the extended SEARCH MUST return a single ESEARCH response instead of the usual SEARCH response. An extended UID SEARCH MUST produce an ESEARCH response with the UID indicator present, which means all the data in it refers to UIDs.

Future extensions may let servers return several ESEARCH responses for one command, and would have to say how to combine them.

For example, SEARCH RETURN (MIN COUNT) FLAGGED SINCE 1-Feb-1994 NOT FROM "Smith" gets ESEARCH (TAG "A282") MIN 2 COUNT 3 as an untagged response. And SEARCH RETURN (MIN) UNSEEN finds the first unseen message, as ESEARCH (TAG "A284") MIN 4.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer comes back as one short note that says which question it answers and gives only the facts you asked for.

sections.title: Working with CONDSTORE
sections.content:
When a server supports both ESEARCH and CONDSTORE and a client combines result options with the MODSEQ search criterion, the server MUST return an ESEARCH response that contains a MODSEQ result option, not the extended SEARCH response from the CONDSTORE specification.

With a single MIN or MAX, the MODSEQ value belongs to the found message. With MIN and MAX together and no ALL or COUNT, it is the highest mod-sequence of the two returned messages. Otherwise it is the highest mod-sequence of all messages being returned.
sections.plainLanguage: If the mailbox also keeps a change counter, the answer includes the biggest change number among the messages it reports.

sections.title: Syntax, Security and IANA
sections.content:
The formal syntax adds the ESEARCH capability and defines the return data (MIN and MAX with a number, ALL with a sequence-set, COUNT with a number) and the return options. Implementations MUST accept these strings case-insensitively. IANA added the ESEARCH capability to the IMAP4 capabilities registry.

On security, SEARCH can be CPU and IO intensive and is seen by some as a denial of service target, so some sites disable it. ALL and COUNT do not change how the search runs internally. MIN and MAX can lighten the load on servers that optimize them. The RFC believes the extension raises no security concerns beyond those already discussed in RFC 3501.
sections.plainLanguage: Searching a huge mailbox is hard work for the server. Asking for less in the answer does not make the search harder, and sometimes makes it easier.
